The CDC, along with its planners and content experts, has disclosed that they have no financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. 2. 3. This document does not include discussions on the off-label use of products or investigational use of products, except for recommendations that may be inconsistent with package labeling. 4. In the United States, unintended pregnancy rates remain high, with approximately 45% of all pregnancies being unintended. These rates are disproportionately higher among adolescents, young women, women from racial/ethnic minority groups, and women with lower levels of education and income. 5. Unintended pregnancies are associated with increased risks of adverse maternal and infant outcomes. In 2010, they resulted in government healthcare expenditures of $21 billion. 6. About half of unintended pregnancies occur in women who were not using contraception at the time of conception, while the other half occur in women who became pregnant despite reported contraceptive use. 7. Strategies to prevent unintended pregnancies include assisting at-risk women and their partners in selecting appropriate contraceptive methods and ensuring correct and consistent use of these methods. 8. In 2013, the CDC published the first U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (U.S. SPR), adapted from global guidance developed by the World Health Organization (WHO SPR). This guidance provides evidence-based recommendations on the safe and effective use of contraceptive methods once deemed medically appropriate. 9. The U.S. SPR serves as a companion document to the U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (U.S. MEC), which provides recommendations on the safe use of contraceptive methods for women with various medical conditions and characteristics. 10. The WHO intended its global guidance to be used by local or national policymakers, family planning program managers, and the scientific community as a reference for developing family planning guidance at the country or program level. 11. Between 2012 and 2013, the CDC adapted the global guidance for implementation in the United States through a formal process that included systematic reviews of scientific evidence and input from national experts. 12. The CDC committed to keeping this guidance updated based on the best available evidence, with full reviews conducted every few years. 13. This document updates the 2013 U.S. SPR with new evidence and expert input. Major updates include revised recommendations for initiating regular contraception after using emergency contraceptive pills and new recommendations for medications to ease intrauterine device (IUD) insertion. 14. Recommendations are provided for healthcare providers on the safe and effective use of contraceptive methods, addressing provision, management of side effects, and removal of unnecessary medical barriers to access and use. 15. These recommendations are intended to serve as clinical guidance for healthcare providers, who should always consider the individual clinical circumstances of each patient seeking family planning services. 16. This report is not a substitute for professional medical advice for individual patients, who should consult their healthcare providers when considering family planning options. 17. Updated recommendations include advising women to start or resume hormonal contraception no sooner than five days after using ulipristal acetate (UPA) emergency contraceptive pills. For methods requiring a healthcare visit, such as IUDs or implants, starting the method at the time of UPA use may be considered, weighing the risks and benefits. 18. Women should abstain from sexual intercourse or use barrier contraception for seven days after starting or resuming regular contraception or until their next menstrual period, whichever comes first. 19. Nonhormonal contraceptive methods can be started immediately after UPA use. Women should take a pregnancy test if they do not experience withdrawal bleeding within three weeks. 20. New recommendations for IUD insertion include that misoprostol is not recommended for routine use before IUD insertion but may be helpful in select circumstances, such as after a recent failed insertion. Paracervical block with lidocaine may reduce patient pain during IUD insertion. 21. Since the publication of the 2013 U.S. SPR, the CDC has monitored the literature for new evidence relevant to the recommendations through the WHO/CDC Continuous Identification of Research Evidence (CIRE) system. 22. The CIRE system identifies new evidence as it is published, allowing WHO and CDC to update systematic reviews and recommendations as warranted. 23. Automated searches are conducted weekly in PubMed, and relevant abstracts are added to the CIRE system for coordination and peer review of systematic reviews. 24. In 2014, the CDC reviewed all existing recommendations in the 2013 U.S. SPR for new evidence that could lead to changes in recommendations. An expert meeting was held in 2014 to solicit input on updating the guidance. 25. The CDC identified one topic for addition to the guidance: the use of medications to ease IUD insertion. Another topic reviewed was the initiation of regular contraception after emergency contraceptive pills, specifically ulipristal acetate. 26. The CDC determined that all other recommendations in the 2013 U.S. SPR were up-to-date and consistent with the current body of evidence. 27. The CDC will continue to work with WHO to identify and assess new evidence and determine whether changes in recommendations are warranted. Updates to the guidance will be made available on the U.S. SPR website. 28. The recommendations in this report are intended to help healthcare providers address issues related to contraceptive use, including initiation, necessary examinations, follow-up, and management of problems such as missed pills and side effects. 29. Each recommendation includes specific guidance for healthcare providers and women in various clinical situations. For women who may be medically ineligible for certain recommendations, comments and references to the U.S. MEC are provided. 30. The information in this document is organized by contraceptive method, generally presented in order of effectiveness, from highest to lowest. 31. Recommendations are provided for permanent methods of contraception, such as vasectomy and female sterilization, as well as reversible methods, including IUDs, implants, injectables, pills, and barrier methods. 32. Recommendations also address emergency contraception, including the copper IUD and emergency contraceptive pills. 33. Many recommendations include guidance that a woman can start a contraceptive method at any time during her menstrual cycle if it is reasonably certain she is not pregnant. Guidance on how to be reasonably certain a woman is not pregnant is also provided. 34. Most women require no or very few examinations or tests before initiating a contraceptive method, although additional screening may be needed for preventive healthcare or to address other health needs. 35. The WHO/CDC classification system categorizes the applicability of various examinations or tests before initiating contraceptive methods into three classes: essential and mandatory (Class A), substantially contributing to safety and effectiveness (Class B), and not substantially contributing (Class C). 36. Systematic reviews were conducted to assess whether specific screening tests were associated with the safe use of contraceptive methods. These classifications focus on the relationship of tests to the safe initiation of contraception. 37. Summary charts and clinical algorithms have been developed to assist healthcare providers in managing family planning patients, including guidance on when to start specific contraceptive methods and how to manage side effects or complications. 38. Many elements must be considered individually by women, men, or couples when choosing the most appropriate contraceptive method, including safety, effectiveness, availability, and acceptability. 39. Voluntary informed choice of contraceptive methods is essential, and counseling may contribute to the successful use of contraception. 40. Contraceptive method effectiveness is critical in minimizing the risk of unintended pregnancy, particularly for women for whom unintended pregnancy poses additional health risks. 41. Long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) methods, such as IUDs and implants, are highly effective because they do not depend on regular user compliance. These methods are appropriate for most women, including adolescents and nulliparous women. 42. All women should be counseled about the full range of contraceptive options for which they are medically eligible to identify the optimal method. 43. Dual protection from the simultaneous risk of HIV and other sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) should be considered when choosing a contraceptive method. Hormonal contraceptives and IUDs do not protect against STDs, including HIV. 44. Consistent and correct use of male latex condoms reduces the risk of HIV infection and other STDs. Female condoms may also provide protection, although evidence is limited. 45. All patients, regardless of contraceptive choice, should be counseled about condom use and the risk of STDs, including HIV infection. 46. Women, men, and couples have increasing numbers of safe and effective contraceptive options, including LARC methods, to reduce the risk of unintended pregnancy. Evidence-based guidance is essential to help healthcare providers offer quality family planning care. 47. Removing unnecessary barriers can help patients access and successfully use contraceptive methods. Examples include eliminating unnecessary screening tests, providing same-day contraception, and reducing follow-up requirements. 48. A detailed history provides the most accurate assessment of pregnancy risk in women about to start contraception. Several criteria for assessing pregnancy risk are highly accurate in ruling out pregnancy. 49. Routine pregnancy testing for every woman is not necessary. However, healthcare providers may consider a urine pregnancy test based on clinical judgment, keeping in mind the limitations of test accuracy. 50. If a woman has had recent unprotected sexual intercourse and does not desire pregnancy, offering emergency contraception, such as a copper IUD or emergency contraceptive pills, should be considered.
